clinicalScope: Immunoglobulins (antibody proteins) in humans, covering normal physiology, common deficiencies and therapeutic use, with emphasis on low‑resource East African hospital settings
title: Immunoglobulins: Structure, Function and Clinical Relevance
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Immunoglobulins are Y‑shaped proteins made by plasma cells that recognise and neutralise pathogens. Their levels guide diagnosis of infections, autoimmune disease and primary antibody deficiencies, and pooled IgG can be given as therapy when the body cannot make enough.

sections.p: Human immunoglobulins are grouped into five isotypes (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD) that differ in heavy‑chain constant region, serum concentration and primary site of action.
b: IgG – most abundant (≈75 % of serum Ig), crosses placenta, provides long‑term protection.
IgM – first antibody produced, forms pentamers, excellent at complement activation.
IgA – secretory form dominates mucosal surfaces (saliva, gut, respiratory tract).
IgE – binds mast cells/basophils, mediates allergy and defence against parasites.
IgD – low serum level, acts as B‑cell receptor on naïve B cells.

sections.p: Each immunoglobulin consists of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bonds, forming a Y‑shaped molecule with variable (V) and constant (C) regions.
b: Variable regions (VH, VL) form the antigen‑binding sites; diversity generated by V(D)J recombination.
Constant regions determine isotype‑specific effector functions (Fc‑mediated).
Molecular weight ranges from 150 kDa (IgG) to 900 kDa (pentameric IgM).
Glycosylation of the Fc region modulates complement binding and half‑life.

sections.p: Antibodies protect by neutralising toxins, opsonising microbes for phagocytosis, fixing complement, and mediating antibody‑dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).
b: Neutralisation – Fab blocks pathogen attachment or toxin activity.
Opsonisation – Fc binds complement C3b or Fcγ receptors on phagocytes.
Complement activation – IgM and IgG1/IgG3 trigger the classical pathway.
Mucosal immunity – secretory IgA prevents colonisation of epithelial surfaces.

sections.p: When antibody production is impaired, patients develop recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections, especially with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.
b: Primary antibody deficiency (e.g., X‑linked agammaglobulinaemia) presents in childhood with absent IgG/IgA/IgM.
Secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia occurs in HIV, malnutrition, protein‑losing nephrotic syndrome, and after chemotherapy.
IgA deficiency may predispose to mucosal infections and anaphylaxis to blood products.
Selective IgM deficiency is rare but linked to poor response to polysaccharide vaccines.

sections.h: Clinical manifestations of abnormal Ig levels
sections.p: Both excess and deficiency produce recognizable patterns that guide further work‑up.
b: Elevated IgE – atopic dermatitis, parasitic infection, hyper‑IgE syndrome.
High IgG subclasses – chronic infections, autoimmune disease, multiple myeloma (monoclonal spike).
Low IgG/IgA – recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic diarrhoea, poor vaccine response.
IgM‑low with normal IgG – may indicate early B‑cell defect or selective IgM deficiency.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, if quantitative Ig testing is unavailable, clinicians rely on clinical pattern (recurrent infections) and response to trial IgG replacement.

t.a: Serum quantitative immunoglobulin panel (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE)
t.b: What is the patient’s overall antibody production? – Values below age‑adjusted reference suggest primary/secondary deficiency; markedly high IgE points to atopy or parasitosis.
Is there a monoclonal gammopathy? – A sharp M‑spike indicates a clonal plasma‑cell disorder; polyclonal rise suggests chronic infection or inflammation.
Does the patient mount a protective response? – Low titres after appropriate schedule confirm functional antibody deficiency.

t.a: Urine protein electrophoresis (when nephrotic syndrome suspected)
t.b: Is there loss of immunoglobulins in urine? – Heavy proteinuria can cause secondary hypogammaglobulinaemia.

sections.p: Replacement therapy with pooled intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or subcutaneous IgG (SCIG) is indicated for documented antibody deficiency or specific immune‑mediated conditions.
b: Primary antibody deficiency – regular IVIG/SCIG every 3–4 weeks improves infection rate.
Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) – high‑dose IVIG blocks Fcγ receptors, rapidly raises platelet count.
Neonatal hemolytic disease (Rh incompatibility) – anti‑D Ig prevents maternal sensitisation.
Kawasaki disease – IVIG reduces coronary artery aneurysm risk.

sections.h: Resistance and adverse effects of immunoglobulin therapy
sections.p: IVIG is a blood‑product; adverse events are mostly infusion‑related and can be mitigated with proper technique.
b: Common: headache, chills, fever, mild hypertension.
Serious but rare: aseptic meningitis, thromboembolic events, hemolysis (especially in high‑dose regimens).
In low‑resource hospitals, use slow infusion rates and pre‑medication with acetaminophen/antihistamine when possible.
Monitor for renal dysfunction in patients with pre‑existing kidney disease.

sections.p: Vaccination remains the cornerstone of preventing infections that would otherwise expose antibody‑deficient patients to severe disease.
b: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) and polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) are essential for IgG‑deficient patients.
Annual influenza vaccine reduces viral‑triggered exacerbations.
Screening newborns for Rh‑negative status and providing anti‑D Ig prevents allo‑immunisation.
In regions with high helminth burden, deworming reduces IgE‑mediated pathology.

sections.p: Untreated deficiency leads to organ‑specific damage and increased mortality.
b: Bronchiectasis from repeated pneumonias.
Chronic sinusitis and otitis media causing hearing loss.
Enteropathy with malabsorption in IgA deficiency.
Autoimmune phenomena (e.g., lupus) may coexist with hyper‑gammaglobulinaemia.

sections.p: When faced with a patient with recurrent infections, the examiner expects a systematic assessment of antibody status and appropriate management steps.
b: History: frequency, type, and severity of infections; vaccine record; family history of immunodeficiency.
Examination: growth parameters, lung auscultation, sinus tenderness, lymphadenopathy.
Investigations: age‑adjusted quantitative Ig panel, vaccine titres, SPEP.
Management: start prophylactic antibiotics if IgG < 4 g/L, arrange IVIG if confirmed deficiency, vaccinate with conjugate vaccines.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever > 38.5 °C with new respiratory distress in a known antibody‑deficient child
Rapidly progressive neurological signs after IVIG infusion (suggesting aseptic meningitis)
Signs of thromboembolism (chest pain, dyspnoea) during high‑dose IVIG

faq.q: Why does IgM appear first after infection?
faq.a: IgM is produced by naïve B cells before class‑switching; its pentameric form efficiently activates complement.

faq.q: Can a normal total IgG level hide a specific subclass deficiency?
faq.a: Yes; measuring IgG subclasses is needed when infections persist despite normal total IgG.
Current evidence does not support routine IVIG for COVID‑19; it is reserved for patients with underlying antibody deficiency.

exam: A 6‑year‑old with three episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia in 12 months – which investigation confirms an antibody deficiency? — Quantitative serum IgG with vaccine‑specific IgG titres.
Why is IgA deficiency often asymptomatic yet can cause anaphylaxis to blood products? — IgA‑deficient individuals may develop anti‑IgA antibodies; exposure to donor IgA triggers severe reactions.
In a patient with severe haemolytic disease of the newborn, what immunoglobulin is given and why? — Anti‑D (Rh) Ig; it blocks maternal anti‑Rh antibodies from crossing the placenta.
Explain the mechanism by which IVIG raises platelet counts in ITP. — High‑dose IgG saturates Fcγ receptors on macrophages, preventing destruction of antibody‑coated platelets.

A patient with HIV presents with low IgG and recurrent sinopulmonary infections. What is the next step in management? — Start prophylactic antibiotics and arrange IVIG if IgG < 4 g/L; optimise antiretroviral therapy.
How does secretory IgA protect the gut from enteric pathogens? — It binds luminal microbes, preventing attachment to epithelial cells and facilitates removal by peristalsis.
What laboratory finding distinguishes multiple myeloma from polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia? — A sharp monoclonal M‑spike on SPEP with immunofixation confirming a single heavy‑light chain type.
When IVIG is unavailable, what alternative strategy can be used for a child with X‑linked agammaglobulinaemia? — Provide prophylactic oral antibiotics and ensure up‑to‑date conjugate vaccinations.
Why is IgG the only isotype that crosses the placenta? — Its Fc region binds neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) in the placenta, allowing transcytosis to the fetus.

A patient develops headache and fever 6 h after IVIG infusion. What is the likely adverse effect and immediate management? — Aseptic meningitis; stop infusion, give analgesia, and monitor; consider slower rate for future doses.

In a low‑resource clinic without quantitative Ig testing, what clinical criteria prompt empirical IVIG? — ≥ 4 episodes of severe bacterial infection per year, poor vaccine response, and failure of prophylactic antibiotics.
